Part 1 · Your heart

Meet your heart

  • Your heart is a muscular organ about the size of your fist.
  • It pumps blood throughout your body.
  • Blood carries oxygen and nutrients that your organs need to work.
  • Your heart works around the clock, even when you are sleeping.
  • Your maximum heart rate is about 220 minus your age. Age sets the most beats per minute your heart can safely reach.

No blood means no oxygen. The brain and other organs stop working within minutes. That is why every beat matters.

What to do

A heart attack is a blood flow problem. Cardiac arrest is an electrical problem. A heart attack can sometimes trigger cardiac arrest.

Part 2 · Do not mix them up

Heart attack vs cardiac arrest: side by side

Heart attack

Cardiac arrest

Blood flow to heart muscle is blocked or reduced
Heart stops pumping blood effectively
Usually involves a circulation problem
Often involves an electrical problem
Person may be conscious
Person becomes unresponsive
Can trigger cardiac arrest
Requires immediate emergency response
Guess each cardiac arrest answer, then click it to reveal.

Important: a heart attack and cardiac arrest are different, but a heart attack can sometimes cause cardiac arrest.

Does a normal-looking rhythm mean someone is healthy?

No. A normal-looking heart rhythm does not guarantee that someone is healthy or that cardiac arrest cannot happen later.

Does cardiac arrest always show a flat line?

No. Cardiac arrest does not always show a flat line.

Part 3 · Why this group?

Why do we focus on South Asian families?

South Asians living abroad have some of the highest rates of coronary heart disease. Look at the difference.

Earlier

Risk factors can start at younger ages.

Lighter weight

Problems can appear at lower body weights.

Not destiny

Risk is not a sentence. Habits and checkups help.

Part 4 (1 of 3) · Click a tab

How do doctors find the problem?

Next: once doctors understand a person's risk, or find a narrowed artery, they can decide what treatment is appropriate. But how do they actually open a blocked artery?

Part 4 (2 of 3) · Step through it

How do doctors open a narrowed artery?

Angioplasty and stents treat certain narrowed arteries. They do not remove every plaque, so prevention still matters.

Part 4 (3 of 3) · Click a card

What medicines protect the heart?

Depending on the person's needs, doctors may prescribe cholesterol-lowering medicines, blood-pressure medicines, or medicines to manage diabetes and reduce clotting risk.

What should families remember?

  • These medicines are not a universal emergency kit. Whether someone needs them depends on their medical history and the situation.
  • If someone may be having a heart attack, call 911 immediately. Do not delay emergency care to find or give medicine.
  • For South Asian families, prevention also means appropriate blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar checks, especially when there is a family history of early heart disease or diabetes.
Part 5 · Prevention starts at home

Protect your heart: prevention starts at home

Heart disease prevention involves everyday habits, early detection, and appropriate medical care.

Recap

Three things to remember

1. Two emergencies

A heart attack is a blood flow problem. Cardiac arrest is an electrical problem. Call 911 for both.

2. Silent risk

Plaque builds up quietly. Feeling fine does not mean no risk. Know your numbers and family history, especially in South Asian families.

3. Small habits

Food, movement, sleep, and checkups add up. Support your family without blaming anyone.
